after.name: Robert E. Horn
works: Visual Language: Global Communication for the 21st Century (1998)
Mapping Great Debates: Can Computers Think? (1998)

title: Can computers think?
subtitle: The Chinese Room cluster

nodes.label: Machines can think
nodes.text: Machines can think. A digital computer, suitably organized, is not merely a model of a mind. It is a candidate for thought.
nodes.author: A. M. Turing

nodes.label: The imitation game
nodes.text: If a machine plays the imitation game so well that an interrogator cannot reliably tell it from a human, we ought to say that it thinks.
nodes.author: A. M. Turing

nodes.label: Substrate independence
nodes.text: Thought is not bound to a biological substrate. What matters is the organization of a discrete-state process, not the flesh that happens to realize it.
nodes.author: A. M. Turing

nodes.label: Universal discrete-state machine
nodes.text: A digital computer is a universal discrete-state machine. In principle it can mimic any other discrete-state process, including whatever process we take thinking to be.
nodes.author: A. M. Turing

nodes.label: Behavioral warrant
nodes.text: Behavioral indistinguishability is sufficient warrant for ascribing thought. We have no better test for other human minds; we should not demand a stricter one of machines.
nodes.author: A. M. Turing

nodes.label: The Chinese Room
nodes.text: A man locked in a room, following a rule book to shuffle Chinese symbols, can produce answers Chinese speakers find intelligible — without understanding a word of Chinese.
nodes.author: John R. Searle

nodes.label: The man implements the program
nodes.text: The man in the room is doing exactly what a computer does: manipulating formal symbols according to rules that are specified purely by their shape.
nodes.author: John R. Searle

nodes.label: Syntax is not semantics
nodes.text: A computer program is purely formal — syntactic. Syntax is not sufficient for semantics. Formal symbol manipulation is not, by itself, a sufficient condition for thinking.
nodes.author: John R. Searle

nodes.label: Simulation is not thought
nodes.text: The computer, like the man in the room, does not understand. It at most simulates thinking. A simulation of digestion does not digest; a simulation of thought does not think.
nodes.author: John R. Searle

nodes.label: The systems reply
nodes.text: The man does not understand Chinese. The system of which he is a part — man, rule book, paper, and symbols — does. Understanding is a property of the whole.
nodes.author: Systems reply

nodes.label: Internalization
nodes.text: Suppose the man memorizes the rules and the symbols and does the manipulations in his head. He is now the system. He still does not understand Chinese.
nodes.author: John R. Searle

nodes.label: Relatively stable argumentation
nodes.text: This cluster is a map of claims someone was willing to put in print, not a transcript of a live debate. Redundancy, concession, and hedge have been pruned. Spatial arrangement is the argument’s grammar — not a layout of a graph.
nodes.author: After Horn
nodes.notes: Authored overlay. Not a facsimile of a MacroVU sheet. Visually marked as after Horn.
